en: The Opening Homage: Salutation to the glorious Hevajra.
Having first prostrated to the glorious Hevajra, whose nature is free from waves [of conceptual thought],
the purification will be explained clearly by relying upon the generation stage.

First, the *sādhana-sūtra* is proclaimed: the worship-circle (*pūjā-cakra*), the four divine abodes (*catur-brahmavihāra*), the supreme (*parama*), the innate (*sahaja*), one’s own chosen deity (*sveṣṭadeva*), the protection-circle (*rakṣā-cakra*), and the resolve upon emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*).
The cremation ground; the peaked pavilion; the causal mandala; the swift transgression;
the origination; the placement; the nature of hatred; the relinquishment; the wheel of gnosis; the consecration; the sealing; the tasting of nectar; the world—
The meaning: the six limbs; luminosity; arising; mantra recitation; the reality of the offering; subtle yoga; the second installation; wandering, eating, walking, and sleeping; and once again—
Arising. By this, the Sūtra of the Thirty-two Means is purified by the marks of a Great Man. || ||

"First, the worship-circle: 'The yogi whose mind is intent upon the welfare of beings'—one whose nature is to desire yoga is a *yogī*. One who desires the fulfillment of the aspirations of sentient beings is 'one whose mind is intent upon the welfare of beings. Having properly propitiated the venerable Guru according to the ritual prescribed in the *Śrī Hevajra* maṇḍala, he sits down completely, abandons bodily pride, and propitiates the Guru with a correct mind; this is 'propitiation. [This refers to] the tradition of the Guru's correct instructions."

Regarding the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*): even when [the disciple] has properly honored the venerable guru, and having been admitted by him into the maṇḍala described in the *Hevajra* according to the ritual procedure, he is consecrated according to the proper sequence and correctly authorized—having been sprinkled with the consecrations beginning with water and ending with the consort-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)—and having taught the tantra through the traditional instructions, and having recognized that the disciple is beneficial and a worthy vessel, he should thereafter reveal to him the ultimate reality, such as the *viramānanda* and so forth; it should be taught after first establishing the meaning of the other terms.

Thereafter, having been properly authorized, the practitioner should follow the sequence to be described in secret until the attainment of the mudrā occurs. "The attainment of the mudrā" means that some slight gain shall arise.
"Having attained the knowledge of reality that is perfectly pure and non-erroneous": it is "non-erroneous" because it does not become erroneous.

However, because he abandons the impurity of this ordinary body and knows the perfectly pure reality through the gateway of knowledge (*jñāna*), that knowledge is the path. He has attained it; thus, he is "one who has attained the perfectly pure and non-erroneous knowledge of reality. And regarding the phrase "one who has obtained the sign" (*labdhanimitta*): the sign is the conceptualized object. Because of the attainment of the perfectly pure and non-erroneous knowledge of reality, non-erroneous knowledge is the cause and the non-erroneous knowledge of reality is the effect. One "obtains the sign" by knowing that sign according to tradition. For this very reason—
Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane;
the lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by his signs.

Furthermore, by the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that once the yogi endowed with knowledge has obtained the root mantra as described, he should go to a cremation ground or a forest, desiring to accomplish the illustrious Hevajra.

Thereafter, having stayed in a delightful place, performed the offerings, worship, and so forth to be described, and having brought the circle of worship (*pūjācakra*) by means of secret yoga according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the worship with the specific distinctions of outer, secret, and essential (*tattva*) worship, and then begin the meditation (*bhāvanā*). In this context, "outer" refers to worship with various kinds of flowers and other such items. "Secret" refers to the meditation on the substances of the pledge (*samaya*) held in the hands of the goddesses situated within that circle. "Essential" (*tattva*) refers to the form of emanation and reabsorption (*sphuratsaṃhāravigraha*). With this [essential worship], whom should one worship? One should worship that Blessed Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*) together with his circle, who has been summoned by the rays of the network of light-beams emerging from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) situated upon the sun in one's own heart. By this, the meaning of "emerging from the seed-syllable situated upon the sun in one's own heart" is indicated.

Then, one should perform the sevenfold unsurpassed worship before him. By this, the wheel of worship has been taught by the Blessed One for the sake of the accumulation of merit. From the accumulation of merit comes the accumulation of wisdom; from the accumulation of wisdom comes supreme enlightenment.
Thus ends the section on the wheel of worship. ||1||

2. Having first cultivated the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*), and subsequently generated great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) characterized by the love for an only son toward all sentient beings; then, seeing all those beings fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra, and seeing them without refuge—just as one would feel distress when an only son suffers—the practitioner generates great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Afterwards, having attained great joy (*mahāprāmodya*), how could the yogi laugh even while considering himself accomplished? Endowed with such delight, the mantra-practitioner should cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

One should cultivate it. One should meditate upon great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), characterized by the absence of all expectations regarding attachment to cyclic existence, the attainment of greatness, honor, and the like. Thus ends the four divine abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*). 2.
Thus having become such, the mantra-practitioner should undertake the supreme practice.
First, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*;
the yogin, standing upon it, should visualize himself as Heruka.

Having established oneself there as Śrī Herukavajra, one should bring to face-to-face realization the meaning of the six syllables. Then, through the instruction of the authentic lineage, one should meditate upon the meaning of the four syllables "Śrī Heruka" by means of the yoga of the samādhi of the Vajra of the Light of Gnosis, bringing it to face-to-face realization; this is the supreme [instruction]. 3.
4. The Innate (Sahaja)

Having discarded this impure body by means of this [mantra], one should begin the yoga of the innate (*sahaja*). Instantly, in the center of the Buddha-palace, one should meditate upon oneself as Vajrasattva—described as before by means of the syllable *vaṃ* and so forth—with the faces, hand-symbols, and other attributes, possessing the luster of a moonstone gem, supremely peaceful, wearing a crown of matted hair, two-armed, single-faced, three-eyed, seated in the vajra posture (*vajraparyaṅka*), with both hands joined in the *dharmamudrā*, standing upon a moon disc atop a lotus. One should contemplate Sahajaheruka, who pervades infinite world-realms, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics. Why is this?
The union of vowels and consonants is the supreme state of selflessness;
this is the ultimate reality of the corpse, the seat of Vajrasattva.

Its arising by means of the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* is not intended. Why? Because of the word "syllable" (*akṣara*), which means "empty. Therefore, since the mass (*piṇḍa*) arises from the non-conceptual, it follows that [the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*] do not apply to the mass arising from syllables. For the purpose of confirming this, the Blessed One stated in the eighth chapter:
"The union of *āli* and *kāli* is the seat of Vajrasattva;
for the mass arising from syllables, the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not intended."
Thus [it is said].

"Having visualized Sahajanātha by means of the term Vajrasattva—[endowed] as before with faces, symbols, and so forth, and possessing the luster of a moonstone gem"—according to this statement—one should begin the section on Dveṣavajra. Thus concludes the Sahaja [section]. 4.

5. One’s own chosen deity. Next, I shall explain the stage of the Vajra of Hatred (*dveṣavajrapada*). Through the application of the syllable *jraṃ*: having visualized the sun by means of the letter *repha* in its heart, one should contemplate a full moon by means of its bindu. Within that [moon] is the syllable *hūṃ*, which indicates the seed of the birth of the world. Having thus meditated upon the Lord of the Three Worlds—meaning, within his heart, the heart of Vajrasattva—in what manner? By the method taught in the Deity Chapter (*devatāpaṭala*).
One should visualize the letter *repha* in one's own heart, and from that, the solar disk.
In that very place, one should perform the *kūṃ* syllable, which has the nature of wisdom and means.
From the syllable *hūṃ*, a black and most terrible vajra arises;
one should then meditate upon the reality of *hūṃ* situated in the center of the vajra’s hub.
Having visualized [the syllable] transformed from the syllable HŪṂ, one should contemplate oneself as being of the nature of hatred.

By means of the sound transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, having transformed all this, one should visualize the Hatred-Vajra (*dveṣavajra*) in the heart. According to the instruction, "the Vajra-holder shall become the essence of Hatred," one should meditate on the form and configuration according to the sequence to be described. The yogi should visualize that body, equal to those [deities], in the midst of the four, according to his resolve (*adhimokṣa*).

According to the instructions, one should meditate upon the Lord in this manner: as having three forms according to one's own chosen deity, possessing eight faces and so forth, and being most formidable.
One should visualize the Lord of the Mandala as arisen from the reflection of sentient beings.
Because of this statement: "One's own chosen deity. (5)

In this manner, one should emanate the protection wheel through the yoga of Hatred-Vajra as a host of wrathful deities in the cardinal and intermediate directions in their proper order. One should emit all of them, transformed from the syllable *hūṃ* and filled with great blazing rays of light. Thus, one should meditate on Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka in the cardinal directions starting from the east, respectively. They are black, white, red, and blue; they hold in their hands a vajra-hammer, a white vajra-staff, a red vajra-lotus, and a formidable vajra; they are dwarfish and pot-bellied; and their heads are marked by Vairocana, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya.

Then, in the corners beginning with the northeast, are Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala. They are deep black in color and hold a sword, a goad, a staff, and a trident. Ṭakki and Acala are adorned with divine ornaments and are graceful, yet have distorted faces; Nīladaṇḍa and Mahābala are as deformed as Yamāntaka. In their center, one should again meditate upon Uṣṇīṣacakravartin above, who is yellow, holds a yellow wheel, wears a crown of Vairocana, and is short and pot-bellied. Below is Sumbharāja, black in color, holding a mace, short and pot-bellied. These four, beginning with Acala, and Sumbharāja, all wear crowns of Akṣobhya. These ten wrathful deities stand in the pratyālīḍha posture; they hold a threatening gesture and a vajra-noose in their left hands, and are to be visualized upon sun-discs on universal lotuses.

Thus, having sequentially dismissed the wrathful deities, one should contemplate that they have gone to their respective places. Having stood before them and joined the palms in *añjali*, one should visualize them saying, "What shall we do? while preceded by praise with the eight-line *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* mantras. Then, having commanded them according to the distinctions of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sumbha ni-sumbha," those wise ones receive the command of Vajradhara. They establish their own emanations in their respective places and, having themselves departed, bind the hosts of obstructors by the throat with the *vajrapāśa*, terrify them with their respective weapons, seize them, and returning, entrust the obstructing beings to their respective emanations in the ten directions. One should visualize them standing facing Vajradhara.

In this regard, this is the host of obstructors (*vighna*): Indra is fair-complexioned, thousand-eyed, wearing a jewel-crested crown, and of graceful form. Yama is black, with upright reddish-brown hair, dwarfish, and pot-bellied. Varuṇa is white, his head marked by a hooded serpent, and of graceful limbs. Kubera is yellow, wearing a jewel-crested crown, and of graceful body. Īśāna is white, wearing a crown of matted locks (*jaṭāmukuṭī*), dwarfish, and large-bellied. Agni is red, his head marked by a crown of matted locks, and of dwarfish stature. The Rākṣasa is smoke-colored, with disheveled hair and a dwarfish body. Vāta is dark-blue, wearing a jewel-crested crown, and of graceful form. Above is Pitāmaha (Brahmā), yellow, dwarfish, pot-bellied, and wearing a crown of matted locks. Below is Pṛthivī (Earth), yellow, wearing a jewel-crested crown, and of graceful form.
These obstructors and Vināyakas, seized by Yamāntaka and the others, should be seen as terrified and agitated, intent on seeking protection.

Thereafter, from his own heart, he should emanate upward a wrathful deity who is black in color, extremely terrible, as unbearable as the fire of universal destruction, and having the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī; having projected him, he should offer him to Yamāntaka and the others, and contemplate him upon the heads of the hosts of obstructors. Thereafter: *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīla vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvadustavighnānāṃ kāyavākcittavajraṃ kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ.*
With this [verse], one should plant the stakes. This is the mantra for planting the stakes.

"Oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīlākoṭaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ! With this [mantra], they strike. All the wrathful deities, having visualized themselves as vajra-hammers through the transformation of their own emblems, strike the kīlas with the mantra for striking the kīlas until they have reached the earth. Then, one should contemplate Yamāntaka and the others as having entered their respective emanations. Thereafter, at the time of unification, one should see the retinues of the Vināyakas as being utterly uprooted by the fire of the wrathful deities.
Now—
having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *ra*, [one should visualize] upon that sun a double vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ*.
And with that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-binding.

By means of the syllable *ca*, one should contemplate a net of vajra-arrows, a canopy of vajras, and a ground made of vajras extending down to the very bottom of the earth (*ārasātala*), as indicated by the statement "having dispelled the obstacles. Thus, the protection wheel is described for the pacification of obstacles. (6)

7. Having cultivated conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), one should thereafter utter the mantra that encapsulates the essence of the reality of all phenomena without exception. In truth, that which is the form resulting from the investigation of all phenomena is the "essence" (*sāra*); that which encapsulates it is the "encapsulator" (*saṃgrāhaka*). *Oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

This is the mantra. Immediately following this, while bringing the meaning of the mantra to mind, one should perceive oneself and the triple world as being without appearance; [this is] the resolute conviction in emptiness. //7//

8. One should meditate on a cremation ground in the center of that [space], wherein is the Wisdom (prajñā) pervading the sky, white in color and having the form of the syllable *e*. "Above that" means that in the center of that, above the sky, there is the earth. One should contemplate the peaked pavilion adorned with the eight cremation grounds, through this certain dissolution of the mandalas of the four great elements in the sequence beginning with air.
Now the cremation grounds are described according to their sequential order:

In the east is the great cremation ground named Caṇḍogra. There is the elephant-faced [deity] of great supernatural power, white, on a śirīṣa tree. Indra is the guardian of the direction; he is fair-complexioned, thousand-eyed, and seated upon the white elephant Airāvata.
Vāsuki is the king of the nāgas; he is yellow. The thundering cloud is of universal color (viśvavarṇa). Mount Sumeru consists of the four jewels. The caitya named Sitavajra is white. (1)

To the south is the great cremation ground named Karaṅkabhīṣaṇa. Upon a mango tree is Mahiṣamukha, black and possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*). The world-protector Yama is black and mounted upon a buffalo. The *nāga* Padma is white. The cloud Āvartaka is of variegated colors. Mount Malayaparvata is pale yellow. The shrine named Kṛṣṇavajra is black. ||2||

In the west is the great cremation ground named Jvālākula. On the *kaṇkelī* tree is the white, highly powerful Makarānana; Varuṇa, the lord of the direction, is white; the *nāga* Karkoṭaka is red; the terrible cloud is multicolored; Mount Kailāsa is white; and the shrine named Saṃjñāvajra is white. ||3||

In the north is the great cremation ground named Gahvara. At the *aśvattha* tree is a fair-complexioned one with a human face and great supernatural power (*maharddhika*). The lord of the direction is Kubera, fair-complexioned and mounted on a man. The *nāga* Takṣaka is black. The swirling cloud is of all colors. Mount Mandara is dark blue. The white caitya is named Saṃskāravajra. ||4||

In the northeast is the great cremation ground named Lakṣmīvana. At the banyan tree resides Gomukha, who possesses great supernatural power and is white in color. Maheśvara is the guardian of that direction; he is white and has a bull as his vehicle. The nāga Śaṅkhapāla is yellow. The cloud Caṇḍa is of variegated colors. Mount Mahendra is black. The white shrine named Cittavajra is located there. (5)

In the southeast is the great cremation ground named Aṭṭaṭṭahāsa. On the *karañja* tree is the red, highly powerful Āgānana; the guardian of the direction, Hutāśana, is red; the nāga Mahāpadma is dark green; the cloud Ghana is of variegated color; Mount Gandhamādana is yellow; and the red caitya named Kāyavajra. ||6||

In the southwest is the great charnel ground named Ghorāndhakāra. At the *latāparkaṭi* tree is the black, highly accomplished Śavamukha. The directional lord is the black Rākṣasa seated upon a corpse. The nāga is Ananta, white in color. The cloud is Pūraṇa, of variegated colors. The mountain is Hemaparvata, white. The caitya is named Ratnavajra, black in color. (7)

In the northwest is the great charnel ground named Kilikilārava. There is the deity Mṛgānana, who is dark green and possesses great miraculous power, residing in an Arjuna tree. The guardian of that direction is Nāruta, who is dark green and mounted upon a deer. The nāga is Kulika, who is variegated in color. The cloud is Varṣaṇa, which is of every color. Śrīparvata is blue. The caitya is named Dharmavajra and is dark green. ||8||

In the midst of these, one should further visualize those of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*): on the left, with their hands busily occupied holding human skulls filled with blood; and on the right, endowed with lotus-like hands in the gesture of grasping various flavors. Following that, [one should visualize] dense forests composed of various flowering trees with fresh shoots and leaves upon green meadows; adorned by flocks of various birds such as crows, cuckoos, owls, parrots, mynas, pigeons, doves, and vultures; filled with various wild animals such as lions, wolves, tigers, bears, and boars; agitated by the fragrances of various sweet-smelling flowers; filled with swarms of various serpents; and decorated in various places with skeletons, skulls, bones, and shards.

Furthermore, in various locations, they were accompanied by throngs of monks, nuns, meditators, meditation-hall attendants, ponds, yogins, yoginīs, male *avadhūtas*, female *avadhūtīs*, male meditators, female meditators, yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, pretas, pretīs, rākṣasas, rākṣasīs, kumbhāṇḍas, kumbhāṇḍīs, bhūtas, bhūtīs, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, vīras, and vīriṇīs, whose minds were intent upon the conventions of the *samaya*. They were filled with hosts of ḍākas and ḍākinīs who had attained various [modes of] laughter, dance, playfulness, embracing, kissing, and so forth. Subsequently, with hearts full of bliss, some danced with vajra-steps; some sang with vajra-songs; some practiced various *samaya* conducts; some consumed the five nectars and the five lamps; and some offered various ritual substances.

One should contemplate the eight cremation grounds as being filled with various beings: some are seen satisfying [others] with food; some are drinking intoxicants; others are playing various musical instruments, such as the *ḍāka*, *ḍamaru*, *paṭaha*, *mardala*, *kṛpīṭa*, *jhārjhara*, lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*veṇu*), bamboo pipe (*vaṃśa*), and cymbals (*talā*). Furthermore, they are completely filled with hosts of gods, asuras, garuḍas, siddhas, vidyādharas and vidyādharīs, mahoragas and mahoragīs, kinnaras and kinnarīs, gandharvas and gandharvīs, and so forth. Resounding with shouts of joy (*kilikilā*), these terrifying and formidable abysses are exceedingly heart-gladdening through the aesthetic flavor of the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*). One should meditate on them as being presided over by throngs of vetālas and bhūtas.

The eight cremation grounds are the purification of the eight consciousnesses. Regarding the "eight consciousnesses": they are the five consciousnesses beginning with the visual consciousness, the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*); and [the metaphors of] the mirror, dream, illusion, mirage, city of the Gandharvas, echo, moon in water, and space. Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of all phenomena, the eight cremation grounds are devoid of subject and object. Thus, by way of the analogy of the eight consciousnesses, the cremation grounds are understood. (8)

9. The Gabled Chamber (*kūtāgāra*) is the manifest awakening to omniscience (*sarvajñatābhisaṃbodhi*). Now, the gabled chamber transformed from the four great elements—wind and so forth—is described. Through the purity of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catuḥ-smṛtyupasthāna*), it has four doors. The four right efforts (*catuḥ-prahāṇa*) are known as the four archways (*toraṇa*). Through the purity of the four bases of psychic power (*catur-ṛddhipāda*), there are four altars (*vedikā*). The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the square [shape] and the vajra-thread (*vajrasūtra*). The five powers (*pañcabala*) are the four corners and the *hā*—

And there is the *rārddhahāra* (half-moon ornament). Through the purification of the Noble Eightfold Path, eight pillars are fashioned. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are the steps, the architraves, the parasol, the chowries, the canopy, the bells, and the banners. The gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). One should meditate on it as luminous by means of the word "pavilion. By this, its essential nature is the reality of the factors conducive to enlightenment; however, regarding its generation, it should be understood as stated [previously]. In its essential form, one should visualize the sequence beginning with earth and so forth.

Now, the divisions of the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣikadharma) are explained through the grace of the venerable Saroruhapāda. First is the arising of the mantra-body; its nature is *sar*—

It is empty of [intrinsic] nature. Therefore, the body arises first. By the word "subsequent" (*anu*), its non-existence is the form of that phenomenon; because there is no arising of that subsequent form as "mindfulness," the prior form—which is the intrinsic nature of the reality of all things—is called "mindfulness" by the word *smṛti*. If one asks how it appears, it appears through an imagined aspect (*kalpitākāra*); without that, the essential nature does not exist in this way. Furthermore, just like a reflection in a mirror, it appears as an imagined aspect with respect to its arising. What is the meaning of the word "establishment" (*upasthāna*)? It is "establishment" because by means of this, one reaches the highest of the high states. The supreme, luminous state is indicated by the word "mindfulness."

As it has been said: "For the sake of abiding in those foundations of mindfulness, one should arrange the eastern gate in such a manner: through the purification of the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the eastern gate; likewise, through the purification of the foundation of mindfulness of feeling, the southern gate; likewise, through the purification of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena, the western gate; and likewise, through the purification of the foundation of mindfulness of mind, the northern gate."

How is it that "it becomes thus"? Apart from form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*) does not perceive; likewise, perception (*saṃjñā*) and the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) would be the same. However, just as a magical illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas, so too do these gateways appear. Thus, form, feeling, perception, and mental formations are constructed by consciousness (*vijñāna*); all phenomena (*dharma*) are also like this. Consciousness itself is false. If it cannot withstand analysis, how [is it real]?

What is meant by "investigation"? The sense is that those phenomena (*dharma*) which are constructed by consciousness (*vijñāna*) are momentary. It can be said that they are false. Therefore, consciousness itself is also momentary. How so? By investigating all phenomena. Just as there is an absence of substance when the phenomena such as pots fashioned from gold and other materials are absent, so too is there an absence of consciousness when all phenomena are absent. For this very reason, consciousness is also momentary. Just as there is no subject (*grāhaka*) in the absence of an object (*grāhya*), so too is there no act of grasping (*grahaṇa*) in the absence of both subject and object. Furthermore, just as the existence of a subject depends upon depending on an object, so too does the existence of the act of grasping depend upon depending on both subject and object; in the absence of those two, there is an absence of the act of grasping. Indeed, the remaining form—the Great Door—is not known without its purity of origin. Such a fourfold door, whose nature is illusory emanation (*nirmāṇālīka*), is to be meditated upon.

"The four right efforts (*catuḥprahāṇa*) are the archways (*toraṇa*); they are the truths. These are: the antidote to unarisen evils; the severance of arisen evils; the production of unarisen roots of virtue; and the dedication of arisen roots of virtue toward Buddhahood. Thus: "The antidote, severance, production, and dedication. What is the antidote? It is the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as attachment (*rāga*). Therefore, there will be the non-arising of the affliction. This antidote is that which opposes the act of arising. Even when [an affliction] has arisen, this cultivation for the sake of its destruction is its severance. Because of that destruction, these [afflictions] cease to exist. From this very cessation, there arises the state free from disease (*nirāmayapada*). Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is the desire to share with all beings what has been produced. Thus, through the purity of the fourfold abandonment, there are the four archways.

Through the purification of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are four altars (*vedikā*): zeal (*chanda*), vigor (*vīrya*), investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), and mind (*citta*). "Zeal" refers to extreme devotion toward contemplation (*cintā*). Likewise, "vigor" refers to extreme aspiration. "Investigation" is uninterrupted inquiry; it is the continuous examination by means of that very [vigor]. Regarding "also investigation": investigation is indeed the process of making one's own and others' forms into that very [state] by its own nature. "Mind" refers to the arising of the form of its own nature, which is the culmination of the mind. Therefore, the culmination of the mind is direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). Thus, the fourfold altar is purified by the four bases of psychic power.

Regarding "the arising of supernatural power" (*ṛddhyutpāda*): that which is the pure form through the purity of emanation has what is called a body that radiates and reabsorbs; this is supernatural power according to one's will. The "arising" is the direct realization of this form. Therefore, without this, there is no entry into the form of the *svarūpavajra*.

The five faculties and the square vajra-line: namely, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Firm conviction, which is the primary grasping of the cause, is designated by the term "faculty of faith. From the second [moment] onward, there is the engagement characterized by extreme devotion; it is the activity of *saṃsāra* that proceeds without self-knowledge, having set aside liberation and reached as far as *saṃsāra*.

"Causing to proceed" (*pravartana*) is what is expressed by the term "faculty of vigor" (*vīryendriya*). In reality, this is yoga day and night; it is in the third [mandala]. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the arising of the form of the aspect through the mere entry of the mind into the discernment of knowledge; that which is expressed by the term "faculty of mindfulness" (*smṛtīndriya*). One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is in the fourth [mandala]. By the word "supreme" (*agra*), the correct path (*samyag-mārga*) is meant. Oneness with that is one-pointedness of mind, which is expressed by the term "faculty of concentration" (*samādhīndriya*). Thus, by means of the four faculties, it is square. It is elsewhere expressed by the word "chest" (*urasa*). Regarding "with vajra-threads": there are five lines and five walls, differentiated according to the division of the five Tathāgatas. In the center of that is the Buddha-palace, equal with everything by the word "vajra. Vajra is equal and indivisible.

If it is established by the term "faculty of wisdom" (*prajñendriya*) that there is no abiding in any phenomena (*sarvadharma-apratiṣṭhāna*), then the walls are equal; that is, there is no mutual distinction among the Tathāgatas. Regarding the phrase "by way of the nature of Vajradhara," one should contemplate the meditation chamber as adorned with these walls decorated with vajra-threads.

There are four corners and the necklace and half-necklace; these are the five powers (*pañca balāni*). They are: the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), and the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). Deep conviction is the first cause. The fulfillment of that cause is "power" (*bala*), meaning efficacy. The fruit is realization. Because it brings that about, it is designated by the term "the power of faith. Having made the mind firm regarding that cause, one sets it in motion; this is the power of energy (*vīryabala*).

Furthermore, even for a moment, no consciousness is perceived there. That which is the yoga day and night is the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). One-pointedness of mind, the non-perception of all phenomena as they truly are, is the supreme path; it brings about that direct realization, and because it is inseparable from it, it is directly called by the term "power of concentration" (*samādhibala*). Thus, the four corners purified by the four powers bring about the fulfillment of the four faculties; therefore, they are the "four powers. By the word "fulfillment," it means the fulfillment of the objective. Through the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), there are the necklace and half-necklace. Power was explained previously. That which is the non-abiding in all phenomena accomplished by the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is the fulfillment itself—the direct [realization].
Therefore, by means of the power of wisdom, the meditation on the necklace and half-necklace as being non-different from oneself has been taught.

The eight pillars are fashioned from the Noble Eightfold Path: the non-abandonment of what has been undertaken is called right view; speech that is non-contradictory is called right speech; not transgressing the ten wholesome paths is called right intention; a mind that does not harm sentient beings is called right action; a mind focused solely on the ten wholesome paths is called right livelihood; a mind of ultimate selflessness is called right effort—effort being defined as the discernment of existence and non-existence; knowledge of the three times in a single moment is right mindfulness; and the single form of the three worlds is right concentration. By these, the pillars are fashioned.

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are traditionally known as the female bird, the step, the head, the parasol, the fly-whisk, the canopy, the bell, and the banner. The constant recollection and mindfulness of the thorough knowledge of the three times is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The uninterrupted awakening to the great flavor [of reality] is called the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The engagement through unceasing great effort is called the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīryapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The absence of delight in anything other than selflessness is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītipravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The perpetual yoga inseparable from emptiness and compassion is called the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*prasrabdhipravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The attainment of the non-erroneous reality is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhipravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). The effortless engagement within meditative absorption is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣāpravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Through these factors of enlightenment, the female bird and the others are said to be meditated upon.

By this, through the differentiation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) up to the limit of the meditation on the peaked pavilion, the perfect awakening to omniscience (sarvajñatā-abhisambodhi) within the first emptiness and so forth has been explained.
Thus ends the section on the gabled hall. 9.
10. The Circle of Causes (*hetumaṇḍala*):
The Perfect Awakening to the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatābhisaṃbodhi*).

Now, the generation of the Causal Vajradhara is described. Within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), upon a double-petalled lotus, the four Māras should be visualized as being trampled by the sun disk [of the seed-syllable] *He*. These are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and Devendra; and Skandha, Mṛtyu, Kleśa, and Devaputra. These four Māras are the creators of the afflictions of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Then, having visualized a sun disc above that, one should double it by means of the vowels beginning with *a*. Through its transformation, one should meditate on a moon disc, which indicates the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Having added the six syllables *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *da*, *dha*, *ya*, and *la* along with the consonants beginning with *ka*, and having doubled them while visualizing them in both direct and reverse order, one should see a sun disc through their transformation; this indicates the eighty minor marks and has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Having beheld the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ* between these two, one should visualize the skull-cup and flaying knife produced from them, marked with the two seed-syllables; this is the wisdom of discerning observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Then, emitting rays of light from the seed-syllables, illuminating infinite world-systems, and drawing them back, they are made to enter into that very [skull-cup].

"One should meditate on everything as one" refers to the knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Having transformed all this, one instantly [visualizes] oneself in the form of Śrī Heruka, which is the knowledge of the perfectly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). By means of these five aspects: through the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), the oblation is seen exactly as it was perceived; through the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), it is made of a single flavor (*samarasīkṛta*); through the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), it is discerned; and again, through the knowledge of the performance of duties, that which is to be done is brought into a state of unity. The knowledge of the perfectly pure sphere of phenomena is of a single nature with all these aspects. Thus is the awakening through the five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).

By this [verse], having visualized the single form of the three worlds, one should then visualize Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Rudra in order at the eastern and other gates; likewise, Vaivasvata, Vittanāyaka, Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin in the corners beginning with the northeast. Thus, having meditated upon the eight seats.

Above that, within the centers of the moon and sun joined together, one should visualize the eight seed-syllables: *gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, and *daṃ*. One should contemplate the emblems of Gaurī and the others—arising from the transformation of those syllables—as a curved knife (*kartī*), a skull-bowl (*kṛpīṭa*), a tortoise (*kūrma*), a snake (*sarpa*), a lion (*siṃha*), an alms-bowl (*bhikṣu*), a wheel (*cakra*), and a vajra, each presided over by its respective deity. Having transformed all these into one, Gaurī and the other goddesses are to be produced and visualized. By this, the mandala to be meditated upon has been described.

The colors and signs of these [deities], as well as their purification, will now be explained. Now, regarding the phrase “with eyes red from compassion” (*kṛpayā locane rakta*): “compassion” (*kṛpā*) is the affectionate state of a single-mindedness toward sentient beings. Because of that, his eyes are red. “With a black body from the mind of loving-kindness” (*kṛṣṇāṅgo maitracittataḥ*): “the mind of loving-kindness” (*maitracitta*) refers to the cessation of the aggregates, elements, and sense faculties. Because of that mind of loving-kindness, his limbs are black. “The purity of the eyes is through the three vajras”: the “three vajras” refer to the body, speech, and mind being free from obscuration.
The four bases of sympathy are known as the four feet.

The "means of integration" (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavacana*), purposeful action (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*). Generosity is the application of the mind toward the inconceivable reality (*acintyatattva*). Regarding that application of the mind toward the inconceivable, just as there is happiness, so too is joy; this is to be understood from the instruction. Just as gold is [verified] by burning, cutting, and rubbing, so too is reality; this is expressed by the term "pleasant speech. Just as there is no practice without body, speech, and mind, so too is it expressed by the term "purposeful action. Consistency of purpose...
By the word "tha," there is what is called the single embodiment of all; this indeed is the purification of the four feet.

The eight faces are purified by the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). One perceives form as empty; one perceives non-space as empty; one perceives the attainment of the knowledge of the beautiful and the ugly as empty; one perceives that which is produced by views as empty; one perceives the attainment of space as empty; one perceives the cessation of consciousness as empty. Thus are the eight faces purified by the liberations. "Liberation" (*vimokṣa*) means the bliss liberated from all bonds. "Attainment" (*āpanna*) refers to the cessation of the knowledge of self and other-consciousness through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

"The sixteen arms are the sixteen emptinesses": internal emptiness; external emptiness; internal-external emptiness; great emptiness; emptiness of emptiness; ultimate emptiness; conditioned emptiness; unconditioned emptiness; absolute emptiness; emptiness of that which has no beginning or end; essential nature emptiness; non-dispersal emptiness; emptiness of all phenomena; emptiness of non-existence; emptiness of intrinsic nature; and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. These are the sixteen emptinesses.

Now the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is explained: all phenomena are empty within; this is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*). All phenomena are likewise empty without; this is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). That yoga which becomes inseparable from emptiness and compassion according to the guru’s instruction is internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). What is experienced through that inseparable yoga is designated as great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). From that great yoga, whatever...

That which is empty is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). For this very reason, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the most excellent among the excellent; thus is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). These are the six types of emptiness. By means of these, the conditioned is unified in all its aspects; this is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). In the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), even the formative activity (*saṃskāra*) does not exist; in its arising, all aspects are united as one—this is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). That which is endowed with the excellence of all aspects is the emptiness of the absolute (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). The emptiness of that which has no beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*) is because there is no distinction from that [absolute]. The emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is because nature arises from the five aspects; "five aspects" means empty of aspects—thus is the emptiness of nature. Since there is no intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the absence of an intrinsic nature; thus is the emptiness of the absence of nature (*aprakṛti-śūnyatā*). Whether stationary or moving, down to the smallest atom, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are included by the term "all phenomena"; that which is so described is entirely empty—thus is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). What is "non-existence"? It is the world.

The perception of all phenomena is, by its very nature, like a whirling firebrand; this intrinsic nature has been declared as the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): "self" (*sva*) refers to one's own mind, and its "nature" (*bhāva*) is its state; thus it is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Just as a cake might be formed when the element of space and the aggregate of consciousness become one, so too has the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) been described. These pure forms of emptiness are proclaimed to be the arms.

Now, the purification of the colors of the faces is described: the first face is black, for the purpose of accomplishing the activity of hatred and for the restraint of the sense faculties; the left face is red, for the purpose of accomplishing subjugation and for the state of the unity of body, speech, and mind.

[The face] facing south is white for the sake of pacification; it is the "pacification" consisting of the identification with the pure deities within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandhadhātvāyatana*). The upward-facing [face] is terrifying and smoke-colored. The western [face] is for the sake of destroying the arisen afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, the four faces, resembling bees, are for the sake of destroying the four Māras, beginning with hatred. The "disease based on the aggregates" is the *skandhamāra*, which is the nature of the aggregates themselves. The *mṛtyumāra* is that which harms sentient beings. The *kleśamāra* is likewise. The so-called *devaputramāra* is the infatuation with women. Thus, the four faces, resembling bees, are for the sake of destroying the fourfold Māra.

The purification of the symbols is now described: elephants and the others are taken up for the sake of pacifying various afflictions. These "various afflictions" are as follows: cough, asthma, insanity, consumption, leprosy, eczema, and diseases such as splenic fever; these are proclaimed to be represented by the elephant and the other [symbols].
Thus are the eight afflictions.

The meaning is: "These beings who bear the burden are supported upon the vessel. Alternatively, the symbol held in the left hand is for the sake of attaining the eight masteries (aṣṭaiśvarya) over wealth, the subduing of the earth, and so forth.
Mastery over the body, mastery over speech, and likewise mastery over the mind;
supernatural power, omnipresence, sovereignty, and the ability to act at will—these are the eight qualities.

(1) Sovereignty over body (*kāyaiśvarya*) is the infinity of bodies; (2) sovereignty over speech (*vāgaiśvarya*) is speaking all languages; (3) sovereignty over mind (*cittaiśvarya*) is knowing the minds of all sentient beings; (4) sovereignty over miraculous power (*ṛddhyaiśvarya*) is seeing infinite world-systems through supernatural powers; (5) sovereignty of omnipresence (*sarvagataiśvarya*) is having a single form throughout the three worlds; (6) sovereignty over desire (*kāmaiśvarya*) is causing sentient beings to long for the state consisting of great bliss through desire—the word *iccha* expresses "desire" (*kāma*). (7) Sovereignty over agency (*kartraiśvarya*) is being the agent as the Vajra-holder; (8) sovereignty over qualities (*guṇaiśvarya*) is entering into nirvāṇa in the form of a profound deity, and proceeding from nirvāṇa in the form of a deity. By this, there is the purification of the marks (*cihna*). What is the purification of the vessels (*bhājana*)?
She is established. The vessel is the bestowing of the rays of compassion; the arms are purified by emptiness. By this, the non-differentiation of emptiness and compassion is demonstrated.

"By means of the *mātrās*, there shall be five Buddhas. Here, *mātrā* refers to the mudrās purified by the five Tathāgatas. *Mudrā* is an ornament: the wheel (*cakrī*), the earring (*kuṇḍala*), the necklace (*kaṇṭhī*), the bracelet (*rucaka*) on the hand, and the girdle (*mekhalā*). "The ash (*bhasma*)—thus the sixfold set of mudrās is proclaimed. The "six mudrās" is perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Perfect knowledge is that wherein there is an absence of [ordinary] cognition; in the absence of [ordinary] cognition...

Whatever is form, that would be right knowledge. The head-garland on the shoulder, composed of fifty syllables, is the head-garland on the neck that demonstrates the path of union (*yuganaddha*) through the purification of the fifty syllables of *āli* and *kāli*.

Now the nine dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*) are described: the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) consists of the singular flavor of selflessness; the heroic (*vīra*) is the dwelling in the charnel ground; the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) is the fierce frowning of the brows; the furious (*raudra*) is the blazing radiance; the comic (*hāsya*) is the blossoming of the face; the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) is wearing a garland of fresh heads; the compassionate (*karuṇā*) is the mind intent on benefiting sentient beings; the marvelous (*adbhuta*) is the illusory form; and the peaceful (*śānta*) is due to having abandoned the afflictions such as passion and so forth. By these—nine...

The Blessed One, who is the causal source, is endowed with the dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*). A garland of five dried skulls upon his forehead signifies the realization that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). His head is marked with a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all beings. He has three eyes in each face because he possesses complete knowledge of the three times, and thus he is the embodiment of omniscience. His hair is tawny and stands upright to signify the burning away of all afflictions (*kleśa*), such as passion (*rāga*). His nakedness demonstrates the absence of obscuration regarding all phenomena (*dharma*). His half-lotus posture in a dancing pose (*ardhaparyaṅkatāṇḍava*) indicates that he has attained the state of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). The joining of his big toes signifies the manifestation of the single form of the entire triple world (*tridhātuka*). The Blessed One is also a false appearance; as is the Blessed One, so too is the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*). Furthermore, due to the unity of their single form, she has one face. With blood from the gods and asuras in her left [hand],...

She holds a skull-cup filled with blood. What is the meaning of the terms *deva* and *asura*? *Deva* refers to body, speech, and mind; *asura* refers to their objects. The "removal" (*nirākaraṇa*) and "rendering dispassionate" (*viraktīkaraṇa*) of these two fill the skull-cup. The unification of the skull and the blood demonstrates the fulfillment of the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. In her right hand, she holds a flaying knife for the severing of all afflictions (*kleśa*). The remainder is to be understood as being like the purification of the Blessed One in the case of the Blessed Lady.

Now, one should meditate on the four wheels within the body of the Vajradhara who is the object of accomplishment, beginning with the *nirmāṇa*-wheel and proceeding as appropriate, for the sake of purifying the four bodies—*dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, *nirmāṇakāya*, and *mahāsukhakāya*—in their true nature.

Now the purification of the maṇḍala deities is described. Gaurī is black; she holds a razor in her right hand for the purpose of cutting through the wrong views of sentient beings who are to be disciplined by Māra, and a red [pig] in her left for the destruction of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra. Caurī is red; she holds a cleaver (*kṛpīṭa*) in her right hand to demonstrate the nature of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), and a boar in her left for the destruction of delusion (*moha*). Vetālī has the luster of molten gold; this means it is for generating bliss in order to discipline those beings who require nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). She holds a tortoise in her right hand for the realization of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and a lotus vessel in her left, which is the very essence of compassion (*karuṇā*). Ghasmarī resembles a ruby, having the appearance of a slightly reddish-black stone; she is for accomplishing the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*) and for awakening those who are to be uprooted. In her right hand, she holds [the symbol of] hatred-purification... [text ends].

The serpent is on the right; on the left is the yogic vessel consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Pukkāsī is blue, for the purpose of accomplishing the subduing [of enemies] and for awakening the *māni* beings. On the right is a lion for the purpose of tearing apart the armies of Māra; on the left is a sword for the purpose of cutting through all dualities. Śabarī is white, for the purpose of awakening peaceful beings. On the right is a monk for the purpose of imparting the five knowledges (*pañcajñāna*); on the left is a *khiṅkhiri* (a type of mendicant) for the purpose of realizing non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*). Caṇḍālī is sky-blue, for the purpose of accomplishing the paralyzing [of foes] and for awakening stubborn beings. On the right is a discus for the purpose of cutting through mere partial knowledge; on the left is a plow for the purpose of uprooting the stains of ignorance. Ḍombinī is variegated, for the purpose of accomplishing the welfare of the world, and possesses a cruel disposition.

And for the awakening of sentient beings: on the right is a vajra to signify the teaching of indivisible gnosis; on the left, the threatening gesture (tarjanī) is prescribed for the sake of subduing all wicked beings.

Now, the purification of these eight postures is being described. For the purpose of severing attachment, [the desire for] learning, listening, drinking, eating, sleep, reasoning, faith, and extreme obsession, the eight postures have been demonstrated. Furthermore, the severing of extreme obsession must be practiced during meditation. Thus, the purification of the eight postures has been explained.

All these [deities] should be meditated upon as having three eyes, with tawny hair standing erect, adorned with the five mudrās, standing in the dancing posture with one leg half-bent (ardhaparyaṅka), naked, with faces made terrible by bared fangs, and endowed with the desire for the Blessed One.

Immediately following this, on the row of deities, one should visualize the lute and other instruments, beginning from the right side of the main entrance, with two goddesses at each junction of the door corners. Their seed-syllables (*bīja*) consist of the first letter of their respective names, conjoined with the vowel *i* and the nasal bindu. One should contemplate that their emblems are produced from those syllables and are likewise marked by them, appearing between the moon and the sun. One should reflect that the generation of the lute and other instruments occurs in the same manner as the manifestation of Gaurī and the other goddesses.

Then, Vīṇā is yellow; Vaṃśā is red; Mṛdaṅgā is smoky-grey; Murajā is white; Mālā is yellow; Lāsyā is red; Gītā is dawn-red (aruṇa); Nṛtyā is multicolored (viśvavarṇa); Puṣpā is white; Dhūpā is black; Pīpā has the luster of gold; Gandhā is yellow; Ādarśā is white; Rasā is red; Sparśā is green; Dharmā is white.

These [deities] should be visualized standing upon moon-disc seats, holding their respective hand-symbols and performing the appropriate mudrās, and purified by the sixteen digits of the moon. By this—beginning from the universal lotus and so forth, up to the completion of the image of the Holder of the Causal Vajra and the circle of deities—the perfect awakening to the Knowledge of the Path is accomplished. Thus ends the Causal Maṇḍala. 10.
11. *Drutāpatti* (Melting):

Now, one should meditate on the subtle nature of the maṇḍala, encircled by two rows of the syllables *rakta* and *hoḥ*. Having drawn in the Gandharva-being, who consists of great bliss and is characterized by supreme passion, by means of one's own light-rays according to the oral instruction, and having caused him to enter according to the instruction—at the very moment of entry—the Blessed One, through his union with his consort (*svavidyā*) in the singular flavor of ultimate, supreme great bliss, melts due to the passion of great desire and remains in the form of a seed-syllable.
Thus ends the section on the swift attainment. ||11||

12. From that [arises] the origination; then the four goddesses, Pukkāsī and the others, thinking "We are without a protector," having fallen into great dejection and being exceedingly longing, awaken the Blessed One with vajra-songs that cause the mind to stir.

In this regard, the meaning of these four verses of arousal (*utthāna*) is stated as follows: "Arise, O Lord, compassionate one," and so forth. "Arise, O Blessed One, whose mind is always filled with compassion; protect me, the Pukkasi, through the yoga of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); desire me! Abandon the meditative absorption on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and [assume] a fluid form. "I have [offered] great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) to you. "Without you, I am dead."

"Haṃ! Arise, O Hevajra; abandon this state of being whose nature is emptiness. Let the task of Śabarī be accomplished! "I have [offered] great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to you. "O Lord of the bliss of passion, having invited the worlds [to you], why do you remain in emptiness? I am Caṇḍālī; I inform you that without you, I cannot go to any direction. I see no direction at all. "Therefore, arise; [I have offered] great joy (*muditā*) to you. "O magician, arise! I know your mind. You stand there having performed a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). We Ḍombīs are exceedingly refined and of one mind. "Do not cause the interruption of compassion."

Thus: "I [grant] to you the dwelling in great equanimity. In this way, the swift attainment is demonstrated through the purification of the four principles: the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), the principle of the deity (*devatātattva*), the principle of the mantra (*mantratattva*), and the principle of gnosis (*jñānatattva*).

In this regard, the meaning of the four principles should be understood according to the instructions of the guru, in whatever manner and sequence is appropriate; it has not been stated here for fear of excessive prolixity in the text.

Now, if the Blessed One were of the nature of reality (*tattva*), then he would arise from the performance of the song of reality like one awakened from a dream; and in that case, there would be the consequence of [the opponent's] position. If the Blessed One, with a single mind together with Nairātmyā, were to become selfless (*nairātmyaka*), then—

What kind of dream does he see? Or rather, how is it that the Blessed One rises like one awakened from sleep? To this, it is said: sentient beings do not know anything at all while in the state of sleep; yet, how is their rising observed? Due to the force of what must be done (*itikartavyatā*), they rise suddenly as if terrified. Likewise, the Blessed One, having entered the meditative absorption of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), does not perceive the cognition of self or others; nevertheless, impelled by the song of reality (*tattva-gīta*), he rises due to the force of the momentum of his previous vows (*praṇidhānāvedha*). Thus there are two questions: "Do living beings, relying on bodily pleasure, not know [anything] during the state of sleep, yet they still exist with a body? Is it the same for the Blessed One? And how is his rising? Furthermore, first the impure body was purified by the Mantrin through emptiness...

[Objection: Because one has attained attachment to the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, of what is this "melting" (*drutāpatti*)? [Is it] of the emanation? Thus, it is not so. Why? Because it is devoid of bone and marrow. These are two questions. Then he says: Initially, there is melting of the cause, but not of the fruit. Now follows the explanation of the means for grasping the essential nature (*svarūpa*): Just as the Grasping Vajradhara is attained through the purification of emptiness and so forth, so too the Grasping Varadharaphala is attained through the purification of the melted state and so forth. One question is thus refuted; likewise, the other is also refuted. Initially, by way of the form of the deity, there is the absence of the impure body. In the absence of the impure body, there remains merely attachment to the pure emanation body. Through the absence of that [attachment], one abides in the form of consciousness which is like an illusion, transparent like liquid nectar or the moon. For this very reason, illusory consciousness possesses aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). Just as an illusion does not know the perception of self or other, [so too does this consciousness].
And yet it performs its function; likewise, the illusory consciousness arises without the consciousness of self or others, by the force of the momentum of long-standing vows.

Regarding the meditative absorption of yoga (*yogasamādhi*), the sequence for arising from it is as follows, through the application of five aspects: "From the liquid nectar, the form of the moon. Through the transformation of that liquid nectar, there is the *bodhicitta* consisting of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*). Among these, the moon is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) transformed from the syllable *A*; the sun is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) transformed from the syllable *Kā*. The seed-syllable and emblem situated between those two are called the discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*). The performance of all [these] together as one is the gnosis of accomplishment (*anuṣṭhānajñāna*).

The manifestation of the image is the pure nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Then, by means of the rays arising from the *bodhicitta* consisting of the five wisdoms, one should bring the entire world of moving and non-moving beings as well as the deities of the maṇḍala, and having made them of one flavor right there, one should behold the *bodhicitta* in the form of an autumn moon disc. This is the meditative absorption of yoga (*yogasamādhi*).
The so-called *anuyoga* concentration:

immediately following that, one should meditate upon the spontaneously arisen Hevajra, who is the transformation of that [previous state], appearing like the autumn moon, illuminating infinite world-systems, joined with the Dharmamudrā, and consisting of the five gnoses. This is the concentration called *anuyoga*. (12)
13. Nyāsa is the samādhi called atiyoga.

Then one should begin the placement (*nyāsa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). One should place the syllable *āṃ* in form (*rūpa*); the syllable *iṃ*, which is joined [to the vowel], in feeling (*vedanā*); one should contemplate the long *īṃ* in perception (*saṃjñā*); one should place *uṃ* in mental formations (*saṃskāra*); and the syllable *aṃ* in consciousness (*vijñāna*), through the purification of the five aggregates. One should place the syllable *ūṃ* in flesh; one should further produce *ṛṃ* in blood; and the syllable *ṛṃ* in the seminal essence (*bodhicitta*). One should place *lṃ* in marrow and fat, through the purification of the elements (*dhātu*). One should place the syllable *lṃ* in the object of form; one should place the syllable *eṃ* in sound; the syllable *aiṃ* in the portion of odor; and again, the syllable *oṃ* in taste. The syllable *auṃ* is in touch; and the syllable *aṃ*—
From the perspective of the *dharmadhātu*. Because these serve as the cause for strengthening [the practice], it was stated by the Blessed One in the ninth chapter:
"In the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) there is Vajrā; Gaurī is remembered in sensation (*vedanā*);
Vāriyoginī is in perception (*saṃjñā*); and Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations (*saṃskāra*)."
The Yoginī of Selflessness abides in the form of the aggregate of consciousness.
Gaurī is always proclaimed to be in form; Caurī is celebrated in sound; Vettālī is in the portion of smell; Ghasmarī is celebrated in taste;
Bhūcarī is known in touch; and Khecarī arises from the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Pukkasi is said to be in the flesh; Śabarī is proclaimed to be in the blood;
Caṇḍālī is said to be in the semen; and Ḍombinī is in the fat and marrow.
Thus is the samādhi called "Excessive Application."
The meditative absorption named Mahāyoga is that by which the placement of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is performed. And so it is said further:
"First is the awakening to emptiness; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable."
The third is the completion of the image, and the fourth is the placement of the syllable.

Having visualized four lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, containing sixty-four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two petals respectively, one should contemplate the moving and unmoving world therein. Then, one should perform the consecration of the three—body, speech, and mind—with the mantra for the consecration of body, speech, and mind as taught in the "Chapter on Mantras," according to the instructions of the oral tradition: with the syllable *Oṃ*, the Body-Vajra;
with the syllable *Āḥ*, the Speech-Vajra; and with the syllable *Hūṃ*, the Mind-Vajra. This is the Mahāyoga. (13)

14. The samādhi called "the yoga beginning with the nature of aversion" (*dveṣātmā-ādiyoga*) follows now; that is, upon that [foundation], within the heart of a sentient being, according to the previously mentioned sequence and also according to the sequence of the sādhana. In that very manner, one should perceive oneself as the perfected form (*niṣpannabimba*), having the appearance of Śrī Heruka—either as a solitary hero (*ekavīra*) in the midst of the four [consorts] or as one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) in union with Nairātmyā, or accompanied by one's own vidyā. Immediately after this, one should begin the three pledges (*samaya*): the pledge of the self (*ātmasamaya*) is the state of Vajradhara; the pledge of gnosis (*jñānasamaya*) is on the sun in one's own heart; and above that is the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the pledge of meditative absorption (*samādhisamaya*).

The two—the pledge of knowledge (*jñāna-samaya*) and the pledge of meditative absorption (*samādhi-samaya*)—are to be understood from the instructions that will be explained below. Furthermore, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the Bhagavatī just as one does for the Bhagavān. Moreover, the more extensive practice regarding the Bhagavatī is well-known through the arrangement of the five families (*pañcakula-kalāpa*) in various successive positions. "Kalāpa" refers to a collection of Tathāgatas. With the syllable *ĀḤ*, one visualizes a three-petaled lotus that produces joy; with the syllable *HŪṂ*, the filaments of the lotus; and with the syllable *HŪṂ*, the arising vajra. One should visualize the syllable *OṂ* in the center of its jewel. Having consecrated the lotus and vajra with the two verses beginning "OṂ PADMA SUKHĀDHĀRA," and having caused the vajra to vibrate preceded by the utterance of the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*), one should begin the act of passion. This is done from within the five [families], through the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) as Vāgvajra.
The concentration called "Initial Application" consists of the stages beginning with the conviction in the first emptiness and ending with the bliss of delight. ||14||
15. Regarding the emission (*utsarga*), which is the perfect awakening to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*):

having understood that this bodhicitta—which arises as the great bliss of the single flavor of wisdom and means—has emerged, the yogi, bearing the Garuḍa-mudrā, should worship it with his tongue in the center of the Mother’s city (*mātṛpura*), preceded by the utterance of the three principles (*tritattva*). In this way, there shall be constant worship of the Tathāgata. Even externally, if the mudrā is auspicious (*bhadrā*), or even if she is not auspicious, one must not act [otherwise]; otherwise, it would constitute a root downfall (*mūlāpatti*).

Thereafter, whatever slight portion of bodhicitta remains, even as small as a fraction of an atom, situated within the pericarp; through its transformation, one should contemplate the Lord together with his maṇḍala and retinue in the center of the goddess’s lotus, by means of the yoga of the churning stick and the churner. *Oṃ vajradhṛk hūṃ | Bhagavatī aṃ | Gaurī gaṃ | Caurī caṃ | Vettālī vaṃ | Ghasmarī ghaṃ | Pukkasī puṃ | Śabarī śaṃ | Caṇḍālī caṃ | Ḍombinī ḍaṃ |* By [the recitation of] "one should emit" (*utsṛjet*) and so forth, the eight goddesses beginning with Gaurī are emitted in order into the eastern and other doors. Having emitted the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady by means of the syllables *Hūṃ* and *Aṃ*, the Blessed Lord enters the Blessed Lady. *Bha-*

And likewise for the Blessed One who possesses [the marks]. From the entry of the Gandharva-being up to the conclusion of the mandala-consecration, there is the perfect awakening to the knowledge of all aspects. ||15||
16. The wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) is the complete awakening to all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodhi*).

Following that, one should meditate upon Gaurī and the others, who are produced from the emission of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Thus, having clearly visualized—as previously described—the wheel of the mandala situated within [the heart], surrounded by the host of vidyās, and filling the expanse of the sky with a mass of light rays; now, one should perform the summoning of the wheel of gnosis. Emitting a ray of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, [one sends it] into the sky—

Having expanded the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) into the hollow space and brought it before oneself, one should visualize it, offer the water for honor and the water for the feet and so forth, worship it, and praise it. With the syllables *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, one should perform the drawing in, entering, binding, and pleasing [of the deities]. Having caused the wheel of gnosis to enter the wheel of commitment (*samayacakra*), they merge into oneness as appropriate, and one should maintain the divine pride (*devatāhaṅkāra*).

Thereafter, one should contemplate the wisdom-ego (jñānāhaṃkāra) within the heart. Although the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra) is like the self, nevertheless, immediately after its entry, one should contemplate the Wisdom Being (jñānasattva)—two-armed, single-faced, red, and joined with Prajñā—within one’s own heart; and within his heart, the Lord of Samādhi. Then, one should likewise contemplate [the deities] beginning with the Blessed Lady and including Gaurī and the others. From the summoning of the wisdom-circle up to the entry of the wisdom-circle, this is the complete awakening in all aspects (sarvākārābhisambodhi). 16.
17. Consecration is the manifestly perfect awakening at the crown of the head.

Thereafter, at the time of unifying the *jñānacakra* and the *samayacakra*, one should meditate on the five Tathāgatas drawn forth by blazing rays of light into the sky, having assumed the form of Heruka and consisting of the nature of the maṇḍala. Praying, "May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me," one should gaze upon them. With those Tathāgatas, their hands joined with the five victory vases (*vijayakalaśa*), they themselves perform the bathing while reciting the verse beginning with "Just as [the Buddha] immediately upon birth... and so forth. One should recite: *oṃ sarvatathatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ*. (17)

18. Following that, there is a sealing (*mudraṇa*), and then a rain of saffron, sandalwood, and various fragrant flowers occurs. The sound of a drum resounds, and with the sound of dance, music, and praise, a clamor from infinite world-systems arises. Once consecrated upon the head, he shall become Citteśa; and the Blessed Lady is Cittāṅkā. One should seal Gaurī and the others with Citteśa, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, and Amitābha. Furthermore, one should mark Pukkasī and the others on the head with these Buddhas in their respective order.

Then Vīṇā and the others worship the Lord with their respective objects. Holding these—the mirror, the lute, the perfume, the conch, the vessels filled with various flavors, the objects of touch, and the Dharmodaya filled with the bodhicitta—Pūpavajrā and the others worship the Blessed One.
Surrounded by a host of yoginīs, you have chosen yourself as your own bride;
with a heart full of compassion, you have adorned the world of moving and unmoving beings and awakened them.
O courageous one, perform this task within the deception of Māyā; may your mind be satisfied in the kingdom of Śrī Harihara.

Thus Locanā and the others praise the Blessed One with this vajra song. The Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyā-devis, Krodhas, and so forth, standing face-to-face in the sky, praise him with the heart-mantras, near-heart mantras, garland mantras, and eight-line mantras. By means of this—from the empowerment up to the conclusion of the praise—there is the "Awakening at the Crown" (mūrdhābhisambodhi). ||18||
19. The tasting of the deathless;
the sequential perfect awakening.

Thereafter, one visualizes in front [of oneself] a wind mandala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*, marked with a banner; above that, a fire mandala arising from the syllable *raṃ*, marked with flames; and above that, a lotus vessel arising from the syllable *āḥ* placed upon three skulls, which is itself empowered by the syllable *āḥ*. Its interior is red and its exterior is white. Within it are the syllables *buṃ āṃ jrīṃ khaṃ hūṃ* and *lāṃ māṃ pāṃ tāṃ vaṃ*. Having transformed these into the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), and having produced them, one sees them topped by the syllable *oṃ*, with a moon mandala arising from the syllable *āḥ*, and empowered by the syllable *hūṃ*. Through the heat of the fire fanned by the wind, they take on the form of mercury. Then, having performed the kindling with the syllable *oṃ*, the awakening with the syllable *āḥ*, and the purification with the syllable *hūṃ*, one subsequently brings forth the wisdom-nectar (*jñānāmṛta*) via rays of light from the three principles (*tritattva*) and merges it right there.

Having caused [the substances] to enter, having unified them, having stirred them with the *hūṃ*-born vajra, and having rendered them of equal flavor (*samarasīkṛta*), one should visualize the vajra dissolved into the nectar. Through the entry of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-nectar, it becomes exceedingly cool. Having thus produced [the substance] and empowered it with the three principles (*tritattva*), one should draw [the nectar] in with the tongue born of the *hūṃ*-vajra and, by means of its rays, cause oneself together with the wheel (*cakra*) to partake of it.
From the tasting of the nectar up to that limit is the sequential perfect awakening. Thus ends the tasting of the nectar. ||19||
20. The purpose of the world:

the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Supreme King of Mandalas. Following that, by means of the yoga of its radiation, one goes to wherever there are those to be trained by manifesting an emanation body for each of them, trains them, and returns. Having withdrawn [the emanations] into their respective bodies and having ripened them through this very sequence, one should begin the cultivation of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-bhāvanā*). From the initial emission up to the end of the purpose of the world, this is the meditative absorption called "Supreme King of Mandalas. (20)

21. Then, having seen the seed-syllable of the Great Mantra King, the Universal Monarch, within the center of the enclosure of the moon and sun, one should meditate upon the six limbs. Why? From the mass of light rays emerging from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated between the moon and sun at one's own heart. Then, first [at] the heart of the Jñānasattva...

One should meditate on the Lord of Samādhi as black; having transformed him and visualized him in the form of a drop (*bindu*), one should see—emerging from the pores of the Blessed One’s skin by means of its rays—the Great Black [deity] together with his maṇḍala and retinue. In the second [moment] he is red; in the third, yellow; in the fourth, green; in the fifth, blue; and in the sixth, white. By this method, one should meditate upon the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
"Having meditated upon the six limbs, one should subsequently release the syllable.

Thus it is said. Regarding the term "releasing the syllable," there is a twofold understanding: the "syllable" refers to the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of the Tathāgatas according to the purposes of pacifying rites and so forth; by the word "releasing," the method for entering the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is explained. (21)
22. Radiant luminosity: awakening in a single instant.

Then, having emanated and reabsorbed the rows of vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) by means of inhalation and exhalation, and having caused them to enter therein and become one—this is the meaning: having emanated the rows of vowels and consonants; from where? "By means of inhalation and exhalation"—having emerged through the path of inhalation as the vowels and through the path of exhalation as the consonants; having purified the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) with their rays; having become one with the moving and the unmoving; and having caused them to enter therein oneself; and having reabsorbed Gaurī and the others, as well as Nairātmyā—one should abide within oneself in the state of Vajradhara, which is non-conceptual in all respects. For this very reason, [the deity is] two-armed, single-faced, and white. Where? "In the midst of the union of moon and sun"—the meaning is the non-perception of existence and non-existence.
The Enjoyment Body (saṃbhoga) is traditionally taught for the sake of attaining the unerring reality;
it is supreme, free from the sounds "hūṃ" and "phaṭ," and equal to the reflection of sentient beings.
And so it is stated in the Kulapaṭala regarding the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga*):
"The great gnosis residing within the body is free from all conceptual constructions;
it pervades all things, and though it resides in the body, it is not born of the body."
And so it is said:
"Just as a form endowed with all its limbs appears most clearly in a mirror-image,"
The body of Vajradhara is likewise always enriched with the eighty secondary marks and the [thirty-two] major marks.

This is the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). From the benefit of the world at its beginning up to the ultimate innate (*sahaja*), there is awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*).

Regarding the statement, "The manifestation of enlightenment as the *dharmakāya* [is] then situated in the state of the seed (*bījāvasthā*)," what is its meaning? This seed is the innate (*sahaja*). Here, one should remember this context: it is to be understood through the four purities of laughter, gazing, embracing, and union. Where [are these taught]? In the *Ācārya*, the *Guhyaka*, the *Prajñā*, and likewise the fourth [initiation].
