By this, the meaning of the distinction between the moments (*kṣaṇa*) is stated: by the word "Teacher" (*ācārya*), the moment of variety (*vicitra-kṣaṇa*) is the first bliss (*ānanda*); by the word "Secret" (*guhya*), the moment of maturation (*vipāka-kṣaṇa*) is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); by the word "Wisdom" (*prajñā*), the moment of dissolution (*vimarda-kṣaṇa*) is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); and by the words "the fourth is again that same," the moment of the absence of characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). In the context of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), there is merely a slight unfolding of innate awareness (*sahaja-cāya*). In the context of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), there is perfect sensation. In the context of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), however, there is the absence of sensation. How so?
There is neither beginning, nor end, nor middle; there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. This is that supreme great bliss—neither other nor self.

Thus, having understood this in the state of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), the meaning is that the Blessed One also enters into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). By this, it is indicated that the three types of gnosis (*jñāna*) have ceased to exist through the mixing of that seed-syllable with the moon and sun. By the phrase "having the nature of nectar," the state of the co-emergent is made firm. "Having the form of a mass of rays" means that one should gradually cause it to become unperceivable, like the flame of a lamp. "Rays" (*raśmi*) means light-beams; "mass-form" (*puñjākāra*) means a collection of aggregates (*skandha*); "gradually" means entry by way of the sequence of the five aggregates. "Like the flame of a lamp" means just as the flame of a lamp suddenly subsides from the lamp, so too the aggregates of the Blessed One [dissolve] in reverse order: from form into form, and into feeling.
Feeling is in perception; perception is in mental formations; mental formations are in consciousness; consciousness is in space.

Since there is no separate category [for them], how could the dissolution of Gaurī and the others occur prior [to the elements]? Regarding this, the sequence is stated as follows: having emerged from the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), one unifies the entire triple world and causes it to enter [the deities] in due order. Gaurī, having taken her own objective sphere (*viṣaya*), has entered the form of the Blessed One. Likewise, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī have entered into sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Pukkasī, having taken the solid element (*kaṭhinadhātu*), has entered the realm of the form of the Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*). Likewise, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī have entered into water, fire, and wind. Even though the dissolution of Pukkasī and the others occurs within the dissolution of Gaurī and the others, a distinction is nevertheless stated: is the dissolution of form and the other aggregates [occurring] by abandoning their own respective elements? Indeed, they are taken up simultaneously. For this very reason, the same applies to Pukkasī and the others. When there is the grasping of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), [this occurs] through the purification of the three gnoses (*jñāna*).

Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmikā, whose forms are the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), are elsewhere described by the terms "light," "appearance of light," and "perception of light. The goddess Nairātmā, having reached both wings [of the heart], has already entered the consciousness of Vajradhara. Why? Because of the instruction: "One should visualize the syllable *Aṃ* within the lunar disc at the heart of Nairātmā; one should contemplate the Blessed Lady, having become liquefied together with that very lunar disc of the syllable *Aṃ*, as having entered the heart of the Blessed Lord"—thus is the dissolution of the Blessed Lady.
By this [process], from the innate [wisdom] up to the clear light, there is the manifest awakening of the dharmakāya. ||22||

23. Now, arising from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), arising is explained. Now, this clear light is the supreme yoga. Regarding arising, it is like the simultaneous birth (*sahaja*) from the *jñānālokavajra*. Subsequently, having placed the simultaneous [state] first and ending with the clear light, so that it may occur; likewise, from the clear light again to the simultaneous, and from the simultaneous again, one should meditate by this very sequence until the attainment of awakening (*ābodhilābha*). "By the sequence of the empowerment of the four junctions" means at dawn, midday, afternoon, and night; such is the sequence of meditation.
Thus is the arising. ||23||
24. Recitation of the mantra.

Thereafter, the yogi, weary from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), should recite the mantra. Even that [mantra recitation] should be performed after arising from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), while contemplating the cultivation, the recitation, and the offering (*bali*). Thus, having first established the supreme [state] and produced the form of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) through the yoga of Sahaja-Hevajra according to the stated sequence, one should then perform the mantra recitation. Having produced the Blessed One as consisting of the circle of ḍākinīs (*ḍākinī-cakra*), one should contemplate the Blessed One first and then the circle of ḍākinīs, according to the previous [method], through the relationship of cause and effect. The offering of the *bali* is likewise. However, in this case, Vajradhara in the form of a wrathful deity (*krodha*) should be contemplated for the sake of subduing the wicked. As for the ritual application (*karmayoga*), it relies upon the six-limbed [yoga].

Then, at the time of recitation (*jāpa*), regarding the recitation of the mantras of Gaurī and the others: one should contemplate the Blessed Lady embracing whichever deity’s mantra is being recited within that deity’s abode, by means of the movement of the Yoginīs. There is the recitation of the Vajradhara root mantra, the eight-syllable [mantra], and the heart and near-heart mantras. Alternatively, one may recite only the heart-mantra of Nairātmyā, or the heart-mantras of Gaurī and the others.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:

having visualized oneself within the center of the wheel as united with Prajñā, one should recite the mantra syllables according to this very method—[syllables] which, having emerged from the mouth of the deity with rays of light, enter one’s own mouth, are emitted through the path of the vajra, and enter the lotus of the deity; then, from the mouth of the deity, they enter one’s own mouth again. In this same sequence, one should rotate the mantra uninterruptedly. This is the *dolājāpa* (swinging recitation).
Having placed the syllables of the mantra upon the sun in the heart, they should be meditated upon as possessing rays and having their heads directed upwards. Thus is the *piṇḍajāpa*.
One should understand with the mind that the syllables of those mantras issue forth from the mouths of the Lord of the Mandala and the Māṇāleyas. This is the *samayajāpa*.

Thereafter, one should contemplate that [the breath] goes upward from the navel. Exhalation extends as far as one desires, up to the limit of non-perception (*anupalambha*). One should contemplate inhalation through the nose; likewise, [one should contemplate] non-perception below, up to the limit of one's desire for the perception of sound. This is the supreme, secret oral instruction (*āmnāya*), and thus is the Vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*). (24)
25. The reality of the offering (*balitattva*), the meditative absorption named *Karmarājāgra*.

Then, having produced the station of the Lord of Wrath (*krodheśvara*) according to the previously mentioned sequence and having emanated the wrathful deities (*krodha*) in due order, one should dispatch them for the purpose of summoning the hosts of obstructors (*vighna*). One should [dispatch] them...

Having sent [the obstructors] away, one should contemplate the liberation of the three cities through the three principles (*tritattva*). Having thus contemplated, having generated the *vajra* by the dissolution of the elephant-vessel and likewise the *ghaṇṭā* by the dissolution of the earth-vessel, and becoming the bearer of the *vajra* and *ghaṇṭā*, one should perform the consecration of the offering (*balidhiṣṭhāna*) for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings. However, according to the difference in sequence, this is done through the application of colors. Having been brought by them to the city of Vajradhara, the Vināyakas are summoned with the mantra beginning "Oṃ inda jama jaleta," etc., by Uṣṇīṣacakravartin above and Sumbharāja below, as soon as they have arrived. Then: "Oṃ ākarṣaya jaḥ" (Oṃ, attract! Jaḥ); "Oṃ padmatraye praveśaya hūṃ" (Oṃ, enter into the three lotuses! Hūṃ); "Oṃ svasvasthāneṣu krodhabandhena bandhaya vaṃ" (Oṃ, bind them in their respective places with the bond of the wrathful ones! Vaṃ); "Oṃ vaśaghaṇṭayā vaśīkuru hoḥ" (Oṃ, bring them under control with the *vaśaghaṇṭā*! Hoḥ). By means of this, the summoning is performed.

Having performed the rites of entry, binding, and pleasing, and having generated the nectar according to the prescribed method, one should perform the *kamalāvarta* and other gestures while reciting the twilight song, preceded by offerings of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and so forth, as well as praises, bali-offerings, and ritual gifts.

Thereafter, immediately following the embrace, having performed the binding of the mudrā, one should visualize the obstructors. There, in the midst of the cities of liberation, in the eastern petal of that central city is Indra, thousand-eyed, fair-complexioned, holding a vajra in his hand, seated upon the white elephant Airāvata. In the southern petal is Yama, staff in hand, black in color, mounted upon a buffalo. In the western petal is Varuṇa, white, with a crocodile as his vehicle, and holding a white water-lily and a lotus in his hands.

On the northern petal is the Yakṣa, yellow in color, riding a man, and holding a *śrīphala* fruit in his hand. All of these wear every kind of ornament and possess jeweled crowns. Yama has a sun-seat and sun-like radiance; the remaining deities have moon-seats and moon-like radiance.

On the petal in the northeast is Bhūtapati: white, three-eyed, wearing a crown of matted hair, riding a bull, holding a trident in his hand, clad in a tiger-skin garment, his body smeared with ashes, adorned with ornaments of all kinds of bones, seated on the moon, and possessing the radiance of the moon. On the petal in the southeast is Agni: pot-bellied, very stout, dwarf-like, riding a goat, red in color, holding a rosary and a water-pot, wearing a crown of matted hair, seated on the sun, possessing the radiance of the sun, and clothed in monastic robes (cīvara). On the petal in the southwest is Rākṣasa: with disheveled hair, holding a small knife and a skull-cup...

The wrathful Dhara-Kṛṣṇa has a frown upon his brows; he stands upon a corpse, seated on the sun, possessing the radiance of the sun. On the petal of the northwest is Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, is dark blue in color, wears a jeweled crown, has a deer as his vehicle, is seated on the moon, possesses the radiance of the moon, and is adorned with all ornaments. In the central square (varaṭaka) is Pṛthivī, yellow in color, wearing divine garments, adorned with all ornaments, holding a jar in her hand, seated on the moon, and possessing the radiance of the moon. The *pretas* stand surrounding Pṛthivī. To the left are the five [deities] beginning with Indra, holding nooses of serpents. All, moreover, stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.

Upon the eight petals of the lotus situated at the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) above, on the eastern petal is Candra, white, with a white mount, wearing a jeweled crown, holding a water-lily (kumuda) in his hand, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a moon, and possessing moon-like radiance. On the southern petal is Sūrya, red.

Holding a lotus in his two arms, riding a green horse, wearing a jewel crown, adorned with all ornaments, seated on his own throne, and self-luminous; on the western petal is Budha, mounted on a mouse, yellow, seated on a sun-disc, possessing the radiance of the sun, wearing a jewel crown, and holding an arrow in his hand; on the northern petal is Śukra, blue in appearance, seated on a sun-disc, possessing the radiance of the sun, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a spear; on the northeastern petal is Maṅgala, red, seated on a sun-disc, possessing the radiance of the sun, with hair tied upward, and holding a lotus; on the southeastern petal is Bṛhaspati, deep yellow, seated on a sun-disc, possessing the radiance of the sun, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a mace; on the southwestern petal is Śanaiścara, black, with tawny hair, seated on a sun-disc—

Sūryaprabha holds a trident; he is seated upon the sun and has the radiance of the sun. On the petal in the northwest direction are Rāhu and Ketu, both seated on the sun and possessing the radiance of the sun; their complexions are a deep black and smoky grey respectively. Rāhu makes the gesture of devouring as he draws in the wheel of cyclic existence (saṃsāracakra). Ketu makes the gesture of joined palms (saṃpuṭāñjali). In the central pericarp is Brahmā, four-armed and four-faced. He holds a triple staff (tridaṇḍa) and displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) with one hand, while holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) with the others. With his remaining two hands, he is yellow in color, mounted on a swan, seated upon the moon, and possesses the radiance of the moon. He wears a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), is stout, has matted hair, and is short in stature. Surrounding Brahmā are the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Tuṣita, Yāma, Akaniṣṭha, and other deities, encircling him.

Below the lower lip, in the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions: Vāsuki is yellow; the nāga Padma is white; the nāga Karkoṭaka is red; the nāga Takṣaka is black; the nāga Śaṅkhapāla is yellow; the nāga Mahāpadma is dark green; the nāga Ananta is pale white; and the nāga Kulika is variegated. These eight have jeweled crowns, human faces, and wear all ornaments; their heads are marked by hoods, and they are accompanied by heroic nāraka beings. In the pericarp is Śeṣa, who is white, wears a jeweled crown, has a human face, and possesses a hood.

Having thus stabilized these [deities] and further transformed them, one should manifest them in the form of Śrī Heruka through the application of the seed-syllables of body, speech, and mind. Those situated above should be seen as having the form of the Body; those situated in the middle as having the form of Akṣobhya; and those situated below as having the form of Vāgvajra. For the purpose of all rites (*sārvakarmika*), their arms and faces should be like those of oneself. Furthermore, the ego-identification for other rites should be performed according to what is appropriate. Likewise, for all of them, the offering-cake (*pūpa*) should be like that of oneself.

Thereafter, having prompted [the deity] with the mantra "Oṃ, accept this excellent guest-offering of water for the feet, svāhā," one should present the argha. Having offered water for the feet at the feet with the *saṃdaṃśa* mudrā, one should feed [the deity] with the words "Eat this offering, smell it," and so forth, and announce the purpose of the rite.

Thereafter, while reciting the *Sandhyā-gīta* and the mantras of the assembly of deities—the Lord (*Bhagavān*), the Blessed Lady (*Bhagavatī*), and the wrathful ones (*krodha*)—and having performed the ringing of the bell and the brandishing of the vajra with the appropriate gestures (*abhinaya*) by one holding the vajra and bell, and having recited "Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth," and so forth: "Oṃ Vajra-heruka, maintain the pledge (*samaya*). Abide as Heruka; be firm for me! Be well-disposed toward me! Be well-nourished for me! Be devoted!"

Be mine! Grant me all accomplishments! And in all activities, make my mind auspicious, HŪṂ! HA HA HA HA HOḤ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me! Be Heruka, the Great Samaya Being, ĀḤ!

Having satisfied [the deity] with this, one should dismiss them. In this regard, the mantra for dismissal is: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*. With the syllable *oṃ* there is the making of the aspiration; with the syllable *āḥ*, the act of satisfying; with the syllable *hūṃ*, the act of satiation; and with the three *phaṭ*s, the withdrawal.
The goddesses are the authority, the commitment is the authority,
and their spoken words are the supreme authority.
By this truth, may they [be present].
The goddesses are the cause of my grace.
Free from attachment to both worldly existence and peace, having shattered all bonds of conceptual construction,
they perceive every state of being in its true nature as being like space;
they are lords of the ocean of mind, overflowing with the waters of most profound compassion.
O goddesses, show me extreme compassion! Act, act!
By means of this [practice], beginning with the six limbs and ending with the principle of power (*balitattva*), there is the meditative absorption named Karmarājāgra. ||25||

26. Subtle Yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*). Subtle yoga is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) known as such. Having arisen from that, one should contemplate a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the midst of phenomena (*dharmamadhye*). Upon its petals, one should contemplate the eight [deities] and their Lord. In its heart, one should contemplate the seed-syllable (*bīja*). From the seed-syllable, one should visualize the tip of the pinnacle of resonance (*nādāgrakoṭī*). For the sake of achieving stability of mind, one should contemplate...

By means of that, one reaches the subtle pinnacle; through union with that as a single entity, stability of mind will arise, without a doubt. By mere stability of mind, one should expand the Tathāgata-array, the vast web of Yoginīs, pervading infinite world-systems. Why? Because from its own sign, one expands the inconceivable Lord, the Master who is the essence of the mandala. It is said that by the word "dharma" there are two kinds, which should be understood according to the instruction. Furthermore, one should contemplate the sign as being merely the size of a mustard seed. This is the samādhi called the Subtle Yoga. (26)

27. Having arisen from that, or having performed the two armors (*kavaca*) through the yoga of Sahaja-Hevajra, the yogi may dwell [in that state]. [This is done] with the words beginning "Akṣobhya in the form of a crest-jewel," and so forth. One should wear the *hūṃ* as a crest-jewel on the head; *hrīḥ* as divine earrings on the ears; *trāṃ* as a necklace on the throat; *oṃ* as two bracelets on the hands; *khaṃ* as a girdle on the waist; and *haṃ* as the form of sacred ash on all limbs. One should armor oneself according to the great oral instruction. Likewise, there is the armor for the eyes beginning with "Mohavajrī," and so forth.
In this regard, this is the armor mantra: Āṃ aṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ aṃ. By means of these, the body of that Blessed One is encased by Vajrayoginī, the Tathāgatas, and the others; thus there are two armors. (27)
28. Having become armored with this armor, the yogin should dwell like a lion through the yoga of the innate bliss-vajra. Where? In the midst of the house of the three worlds. And so it is said:
"This is a peaked pavilion, not the triple world; these living beings are not [ordinary] beings, but Jinas."
I am the Lord of the Mandala, not a human being; neither are the sense objects, nor the sense faculties, nor the earth and other elements.
Nor are form and the rest [mere phenomena], for by their very nature they are the Dharma-reality; these are the deities of the mandala.
O mind, as you contemplate the entire universe as the mandala-circle, why do you wander in delusion?
Dwelling. ||28||

29. Thereafter, whatever food or edible substance has been acquired or obtained by the yogin, he should purify all of that according to the previously described procedure for tasting nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), empower it with the three principles (*tritattva*), and then eat it. [This concludes] the section on eating. 29.

30. Having thus explained the procedure for consumption (*bhakṣaṇavidhi*) and conduct (*caraṇa*), I shall now describe the abiding and the conduct in accordance with the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*). For it is said:
"One should avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, and shameful actions."
Having abandoned sleep and the self, the practice is performed; of this there is no doubt.
Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the practice;
therefore, no gift is given through a deliberation on what is a portion and what is not a portion.
One should consume whatever food, soft sustenance, or drink is obtained;
in this matter, one should not form attachments based on the conceptualization of the desirable and the undesirable.
That which is endowed with five colors is conceived as a single color;
indeed, by means of many colors, no distinction whatsoever arises.
Meditation is said to be auspicious when performed under a solitary tree or in a cremation ground,
likewise at night in a mother’s house, or else in a desolate wilderness.
If, when some degree of warmth has been attained, one desires to engage in the conduct,
and if one wishes to reach accomplishment, one should practice by means of this very conduct.

And others say: "The practice of conduct (*caryācaraṇa*) is that which is clearly practiced at the root. Abiding, worldly activity, and conduct are what is spoken of as the ultimate truth. Having attained the most superior [level], what is the meaning of "most superior"? It means one who has attained a slight degree of "heat" (*ūṣma*). When mild, one should move about secretly in one's own place during the night, and so on, until some slight gain is achieved.
Why? Because of the statement: "So that no disclosure occurs. Once the gain is present, whether one establishes a fixed rule or not is entirely up to one's own discretion.
Thus ends the section on conduct. ||30||

31. Then, at the subsequent twilight, with the desire to lie down, one should lie down after bringing to mind the yoga of the end of cessation (*viramāntayoga*). Thus [ends] the section on lying down. 31.

32. Furthermore, regarding the arousal [of the mind]: at the time of arousal, having been exhorted by the songs of the *pukkasyā*s and others, one should arise and act accordingly in this very sequence until the attainment of the maṇḍala-circle (*maṇḍalacakra*). Without that, great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) would not occur. For this very reason: "Just as the arisen [nature] is not known without the generation stage (*utpattikrama*)."
Likewise, without the yoga of the arisen, there is no stage of generation.
And thus:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Vajradharas relies upon two sequences."

Thus, as previously described, he is situated within the mandala circle. He has one face, purified by non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). He has two arms, purified by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*). In his right hand he holds a vajra, which symbolizes indivisible gnosis; in his left, a skull-cup (*kapāla*) and a vajra-khaṭvāṅga. The khaṭvāṅga is the very nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the skull-cup symbolizes the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Thus, he has four arms for the purpose of destroying the four Māras; he is single-faced, purified by inconceivable gnosis. In his first right hand is a *vajra*, which establishes the path of union (*yuganaddha*). In his first left hand is a skull-cup (*kapāla*) filled with the blood of gods and asuras. By the term "gods and asuras" is meant existence and non-existence; by the term "blood" is meant their unification; by the term "filled" is meant the attainment of that state. This is the purified human skull. With his remaining two arms, he is embraced by Vajravārāhī.

Thus, he has six arms, purified by the six perfections; three faces, which establish the self-nature of body, speech, and mind upon their respective lotuses. In the left hands, there is a bell, purified by emptiness, and a trident for the purpose of cutting through the three types of ignorance. In the right hands, there is a vajra, purified by the wisdom of equality, and a flaying knife for the severing of all ignorance without exception.

Thus, the posture of the two-armed, four-armed, and six-armed [forms] is seated half-lotus upon a corpse on a sun disk. Furthermore, as it is for the sixteen-armed [form], so it is for these three as well. This is another mode of arising. ||32||
This concluding commentary on the *Śrīmatsaroruhapādoddeśasūtra* has been annotated by me, known as Jālandhari, relying upon the noble speech [of the Master].
Having composed this *Viśuddhikramatippaṇī* with the vajra of aesthetic delight (*surata*),
may the entire world thereby reach the further shore of the glorious wisdom of the Vajra.

Thus ends the *Vajrapradīpa*, the purification of the commentary on the *Śrīhevajrasādhana* composed by the master Saroruhapāda. This work is the composition of the scholar and master, the venerable Suratapāda.
